title: Given a set of meetings with start and end times, find the minimum number of rooms needed so that no two overlapping meetings share a room.
shortTitle: Minimum Meeting Rooms Required (Interval Scheduling with a Heap)

s1_definition.profdef: This problem asks for the maximum number of meetings that are ever simultaneously in progress, which equals the minimum number of rooms needed. One clean solution sorts meetings by start time and uses a min-heap of end times: for each meeting you free any room whose meeting has already ended, then occupy a room, and the heap's size at its peak is the answer. Sorting dominates at n log n with heap operations also logarithmic.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India schedules many customer advisory sessions, each with a start and end, and needs the fewest consultation rooms so no two overlapping sessions clash. A coordinator processes sessions in start-time order, keeping a tray of "busy until" times, one per occupied room. Before seating a new session she removes any room from the tray whose session has already finished, since that room is now free. Then she seats the new session, adding its finish time to the tray. The largest the tray ever grows is the number of rooms she must have.
s1_definition.oneliner: Sort by start, use a min-heap of end times, free finished rooms before each meeting, and the peak heap size is the room count.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** This problem asks for the maximum number of meetings that are ever simultaneously in progress, which equals the minimum number of rooms needed. One clean solution sorts meetings by start time and uses a min-heap of end times: for each meeting you free any room whose meeting has already ended, then occupy a room, and the heap's size at its peak is the answer. Sorting dominates at n log n with heap operations also logarithmic.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India schedules many customer advisory sessions, each with a start and end, and needs the fewest consultation rooms so no two overlapping sessions clash. A coordinator processes sessions in start-time order, keeping a tray of "busy until" times, one per occupied room. Before seating a new session she removes any room from the tray whose session has already finished, since that room is now free. Then she seats the new session, adding its finish time to the tray. The largest the tray ever grows is the number of rooms she must have.

**One line to remember:** Sort by start, use a min-heap of end times, free finished rooms before each meeting, and the peak heap size is the room count.

sections.s2_technical:
The core insight is that the minimum number of rooms equals the maximum overlap, the greatest number of meetings active at any single instant. So the problem is really about measuring peak concurrency, and there are two standard ways to do it.

The heap method sorts meetings by start time, then processes them in order. A min-heap holds the end times of meetings currently occupying rooms, with the soonest-ending meeting at the root. For each new meeting, you first check the heap root: if its earliest end time is less than or equal to the new meeting's start, that room has freed up, so you poll it. Then you offer the new meeting's end time, occupying a room. Because you only ever free rooms that genuinely ended before the new meeting starts, the heap size at any moment is the number of concurrent meetings, and its maximum over the run is the answer. In code the free-then-occupy is `if (!heap.isEmpty() && heap.peek() <= start) heap.poll(); heap.offer(end);`.

The alternative is the two-pointer sweep: separate and sort all start times and all end times, then walk a pointer through each. Every time the next event is a start you increment a running room count and update the maximum; every time it is an end you decrement. The peak running count is the answer. This avoids the heap and is often called the chronological ordering method. Both are n log n because of the sort, and both compute the same peak concurrency.

A senior-level nuance is the tie-handling and the applications. When a meeting ends exactly as another starts, whether they can share a room depends on the convention, and the less-than-or-equal test in the heap decides it. This exact problem models CPU or thread scheduling, connection-pool sizing, airport gate assignment, and any resource-allocation question about peak simultaneous demand. Recognising that "minimum rooms equals maximum overlap" is the key conceptual leap interviewers look for.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India books customer advisory sessions throughout the day and must provision the minimum number of consultation rooms so no two overlapping sessions collide. This is exactly the minimum-meeting-rooms problem, which equals the peak number of concurrent sessions.

Problem 2 — A room must be reused as soon as its session ends, so before seating a new session we must release any room whose session has already finished; otherwise we would over-provision. The min-heap of end times, checked against each new start, releases finished rooms precisely.

In our mini-project we build a `RoomPlanner` that computes the minimum rooms from session intervals using a sorted sweep plus a min-heap of end times. The demo plans a set of overlapping sessions and logs the required room count.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: four sessions in minutes, zero to thirty, five to ten, fifteen to twenty, twenty five to forty.

Step 1: Sort by start time. The order is zero to thirty, five to ten, fifteen to twenty, twenty five to forty.

Step 2: Process zero to thirty. The heap is empty, so nothing is freed. Offer the end time thirty. The heap now holds thirty, so one room is in use and the peak is one.

Step 3: Process five to ten. The heap root is thirty, which is not less than or equal to the start five, so no room frees. Offer ten. The heap holds ten and thirty, so two rooms are in use and the peak rises to two.

Step 4: Process fifteen to twenty. The heap root is ten, which is less than or equal to the start fifteen, so that room has freed; poll it. Offer twenty. The heap holds twenty and thirty, so two rooms are in use and the peak stays two.

Step 5: Process twenty five to forty. The heap root is twenty, which is less than or equal to the start twenty five, so that room frees; poll it. Offer forty. The heap holds thirty and forty, so two rooms are in use and the peak stays two.

Step 6: All sessions processed. The peak heap size was two, so the bank needs a minimum of two consultation rooms, which matches the maximum overlap between the zero-to-thirty session and the sessions running inside it.

```
[2026-10-26 23:39:01] INFO    Minimum consultation rooms: 2
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  sessions sorted by start: [0,30] [5,10] [15,20] [25,40]
  min-heap = end times of busy rooms

  [0,30]  heap{30}            in use=1  peak=1
  [5,10]  30>5 no free; offer10  heap{10,30}  in use=2  peak=2
  [15,20] 10≤15 free; offer20    heap{20,30}  in use=2  peak=2
  [25,40] 20≤25 free; offer40    heap{30,40}  in use=2  peak=2

  answer = peak = 2  (= max overlap)
```

```
      Insight: min rooms == max overlap (peak concurrency)

  ── State Diagram: Room reuse ────────────────────────────

  [new start] ──heap.peek ≤ start──→ poll (free a room)
  [then]     ──→ offer(end) (occupy); peak = max(peak, size)
  [end] ──→ return peak

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. minRooms: sort by start
  2.   for each session: if heap.peek()≤start → poll
  3.     offer(end); peak = max(peak, heap.size())
  4.   return peak
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The minimum number of meeting rooms needed equals the maximum number of meetings that are ever simultaneously in progress, so the problem is really about measuring peak concurrency. Recognising that "minimum rooms equals maximum overlap" is the key conceptual leap, and once I have it, the implementation follows naturally.

My go-to solution sorts the meetings by start time and uses a min-heap holding the end times of meetings that currently occupy rooms, with the soonest-ending meeting at the root. I process meetings in start order, and for each one I first look at the heap root: if its earliest end time is at or before the new meeting's start, that room has freed up, so I poll it. Then I offer the new meeting's end time to occupy a room. Because I only ever free rooms that genuinely ended before the new meeting begins, the heap size at any moment is the number of concurrent meetings, and the maximum heap size over the whole run is the answer. The cost is n log n, dominated by the sort.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to provision the minimum number of customer advisory rooms across a day of bookings, so no two overlapping sessions collided while we did not over-provision rooms. Freeing a room the instant its session ended, by checking the heap root against each new start, was what kept the room count minimal rather than inflated.

The senior-level point I make is that there is an equally good two-pointer alternative, the chronological sweep, where I separate and sort all start times and all end times, then walk both, incrementing a running room count on each start and decrementing on each end, tracking the peak. I also note that the less-than-or-equal test decides the tie case where one meeting ends exactly as another starts, and that this exact model drives CPU and thread scheduling, connection-pool sizing, and airport gate assignment, so it is a genuine resource-allocation pattern rather than a toy.
